ai.definition: Perovskite-silicon tandems are a type of photovoltaic technology that combines perovskite and silicon layers to create highly efficient solar cells by capturing more of the solar spectrum.
ai.howItWorks: The perovskite layer, with its wide bandgap, captures high-energy blue photons, while the underlying silicon layer handles lower-energy red photons. This stacking allows for a broader range of light absorption compared to single-layer silicon cells.
ai.problemSolved: Improving the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of solar panels by utilizing perovskite materials that can capture more of the solar spectrum than traditional silicon alone.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves depositing thin layers of perovskite on top of a silicon substrate, typically through solution-based methods like spin coating or inkjet printing. This allows for potentially lower-cost production compared to traditional crystalline silicon processes.
ai.buildProcess: First, the silicon wafer is prepared and cleaned. Perovskite precursor solutions are then applied using techniques such as spin coating or slot-die coating. The perovskite film is annealed to form the desired crystal structure before additional layers of perovskite can be deposited for tandem cells.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the stability and efficiency of perovskites, which are still improving, and the scalability of production methods such as solution processing versus vacuum deposition techniques used in silicon manufacturing.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to continue maturing with improvements in stability and efficiency, leading to broader adoption in high-efficiency solar panel markets.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for perovskite-silicon tandems are still developing. Current regulations focus on the environmental impact of perovskites during manufacturing and disposal, as well as safety concerns related to lead content in some perovskite formulations.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include the potential toxicity of perovskites, particularly those containing lead. Technical risks involve achieving stable performance over long periods and integrating perovskites with silicon without degradation issues.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently limited by higher R&D costs and lower production volumes but is expected to improve as manufacturing processes become more established and efficiency gains are realized.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on enhancing the stability of perovskite materials, reducing cost through improved manufacturing techniques, and addressing environmental concerns related to lead content.

glossary.def: A class of materials with a specific crystal structure that can be used in solar cells due to their ability to absorb and convert light efficiently.

Photovoltaic cells composed of multiple layers, each optimized for different parts of the solar spectrum. In perovskite-silicon tandems, this means combining silicon with a perovskite layer to capture more light.

subsystems.name: Silicon bottom cell
subsystems.role: absorbs infrared and red light that passes through the perovskite, and provides the mechanical and electrical base.
parts: n-type silicon wafer (often TOPCon or heterojunction)

subsystems.name: Perovskite top cell
subsystems.role: a wide-bandgap absorber, tuned to around 1.6–1.7 eV, that harvests the blue and green photons silicon cannot use well.
parts: perovskite absorber layer (lead halide with mixed organic cations)

subsystems.name: Charge transport and interconnect
subsystems.role: selectively extracts electrons and holes and, in a two-terminal stack, joins the two cells electrically.

subsystems.name: Contacts and light management
subsystems.role: collects current across the whole cell while letting light through to the layers below.
parts: transparent conductive oxide (indium tin oxide or similar)

subsystems.name: Encapsulation
subsystems.role: keeps out moisture and oxygen and filters ultraviolet light, which are what destroy a perovskite layer.
parts: front glass and rear glass or backsheet

subsystems.name: Coating and lamination line
subsystems.role: turns the stack into a module at speed and without damage.

buildSteps.title: Make the silicon bottom cell
buildSteps.detail: Wafers are textured, doped and passivated into finished high-efficiency silicon cells, then their front surface is flattened or re-textured so a thin perovskite layer can coat it evenly.

buildSteps.title: Deposit the interconnect and transport layers
buildSteps.detail: Thin layers that select charge carriers and join the two sub-cells are deposited on the silicon, often by sputtering or atomic layer deposition.

buildSteps.title: Coat the perovskite
buildSteps.detail: A precursor ink of lead halide salts and organic cations is spread over the cell — by spin coating in the lab, or slot-die coating or hybrid evaporation on a production line — then dried and annealed so it crystallises into a uniform film about half a micrometre thick.

buildSteps.title: Add the top transport and electrode layers
buildSteps.detail: The electron or hole transport layer is coated, then a transparent conductive oxide is sputtered gently enough not to damage the perovskite beneath it.

buildSteps.title: Metallise and isolate
buildSteps.detail: Metal fingers and busbars are printed or plated to carry current out, and the cell edges are cleaned and isolated.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate and laminate
buildSteps.detail: The stack is sealed between glass panes with an edge seal and a UV-blocking encapsulant — the step that decides whether the module survives outdoors.

buildSteps.title: Flash-test and light-soak
buildSteps.detail: Finished modules are measured under standard test conditions, then exposed to light and heat for days to screen out cells that degrade, and binned by output.

prerequisites.why: the tandem adds to an already good bottom cell; on a mediocre one the gain is smaller.
spin coating works in the lab but wastes ink and is too slow for factories; slot-die and evaporation are being proven on pilot lines.
perovskites degrade with moisture, heat, light and ultraviolet, and a commercial module must last 25 years, not months.
sputtering the top electrode is an energetic process that can ruin the perovskite underneath.
most high-performing perovskites contain lead, so end-of-life recovery and safe manufacturing must be built in.

pathway.milestone: pilot production of two-terminal tandem modules on full-size wafers
pathway.unlocks: real field and factory data on yield, stability and cost.

pathway.milestone: tandem modules in utility-scale demonstration plants alongside silicon panels
pathway.unlocks: evidence that they out-produce standard modules over years, not weeks.

pathway.milestone: mechanically stacked four-terminal tandems and first commercial-scale lines
pathway.unlocks: easier integration with existing silicon lines, since each sub-cell is made and tested separately.
cells well beyond silicon's theoretical ceiling, with lighter, flexible modules.
